summary.value: Shamo is the Japanese name for a family of large game fowl. Their ancestors came to Japan from Siam, now Thailand, in the early 1600s, and the name comes from that old country name. Japan protected the breed by law in 1941, and regional types range from the big O-Shamo to the medium Chu-Shamo and smaller birds. The Shamo stands very upright, often near 30 inches tall, with a wide muscular body, yellow legs, a pea comb, pearl eyes and hard, sparse feathers that leave skin showing. The US standard calls for 11 pound males and 7 pound females. Hens are fair to poor layers of light brown eggs but devoted mothers. Shamos are friendly with people yet fight other birds of the same sex, so roosters must be kept apart. They rarely fly and need room to forage. Most are kept for show or as curiosities.
